title: Holiday Package Theft: Best Cameras to Catch Porch Pirates
excerpt: Porch pirates strike in seconds. Aim for faces and plates, tune motion and night mode, and save usable clips before loop recording erases them.
author: HiddenCameras Editorial Team
authorBio: The HiddenCameras.tv editorial team researches and writes about security cameras, surveillance technology, and home safety.
body:
A porch pirate camera has one job: produce footage that identifies a person, a package, and a sequence of events. Not a shadow crossing a railing, not a three-second clip of a tree. The best cameras for catching porch pirates are the ones positioned to capture a face or a license plate before, during, and after the theft, and the ones you can pull footage from while it still matters.

This is a detection article, not a buying article. Below: what the footage must show, where to aim it, and how to store it so a clip survives long enough to become evidence.

What footage actually identifies a thief

Police reports and insurance claims hinge on three things: a face, a vehicle, or both. A clip that shows a package vanishing with nobody in frame helps nobody. Prioritize the path from the street to the door, because that is where a thief pauses, grabs, and leaves, usually heading back toward a waiting car.

Angle beats resolution. A 1080p camera ten feet from the door usually reads faces more clearly than a 4K camera mounted high and aimed at the road, because faces only resolve when the subject is close and lit. Our resolution and distance guide covers those tradeoffs in depth.

Aim at the three spots that matter

Cover a triangle: the door, the drop point where carriers leave packages, and the approach path. If your porch faces the street, the approach path is the most valuable view because it captures plates. If it faces a parking lot, aim at the exit lane instead.

  • Mount near head height, angled slightly down, so faces appear instead of hats.
  • Avoid backlight: pointing into the setting sun or a bright doorway turns everyone into a silhouette.
  • Clear obstructions: railings, planters, and furniture create blind pockets a thief will happily use.

Three setups for three homes

Apartment with a shared entry

A compact camera aimed at your own door covers the doormat and the approach from inside your unit or a window. Recording a shared hallway raises consent issues, so check with your landlord before pointing anything at common areas.

House with a front porch

A doorbell camera plus one porch camera gives two angles on the same event, which matters when one view is blocked by a pillar or a delivery driver's body. The second angle is also what catches a thief who circles back for the box.

Driveway or gate drop

When carriers leave packages by the garage, the driveway becomes the drop point. Aim at the driveway exit rather than the garage door, so a person leaving with a box stays on camera the whole way. See our garage and driveway camera guide for placement details.

Motion-triggered or always recording

Motion-only recording saves storage, but a fast thief can finish the grab before the camera wakes, leaving you a clip of a retreating back instead of a face. Continuous recording, where the camera supports it, or a pre-event buffer closes that gap. Many doorbells keep a short pre-roll clip; check whether yours does and switch it on.

Winter light works against your camera

Most package theft peaks when daylight is shortest. A camera that read faces cleanly in summer can produce useless silhouettes in December, because deliveries keep arriving after sunset and the porch light becomes the only light that matters. Test your setup after dark, not at noon, and look at what the footage actually shows: faces lit from above by a bare bulb wash out, while faces lit from the front stay readable.

Leave the porch light on through the delivery window and make sure it falls on visitors' faces rather than shining straight into the lens, which causes glare that hides more than darkness does. If the camera switches to night mode, check that infrared reflecting off a nearby wall or a parcel does not white out the frame. Wipe the lens before the holiday rush; a thin film of dust scatters infrared and softens every night clip. One dark-evening walk-through tells you more than a week of daytime alerts.

Make the footage usable as evidence

  1. Sync the camera's clock with network time so clips match shipping notifications.
  2. Keep the original file; export a copy and never trim or re-encode the original.
  3. Note the exact theft window from tracking updates before filing a report.
  4. Ask neighbors promptly whether their cameras caught the same approach path; overlapping angles often supply the plate or face your camera missed.
  5. Back up to a second device or cloud account so loop recording cannot overwrite the event.

Run this check before the next holiday

Place a box on the porch, walk the approach yourself, and confirm three things: the alert arrives, the clip shows your face, and the file is where you think it is. Adjust the angle once, now, while the stakes are zero. Then read our full porch pirate walkthrough for evidence handling and reporting steps.
